note.en: What you see: Advanced into the stomach with the tip flexed upward, the probe looks back at the heart from below so the left ventricle appears as a round doughnut in cross section. The anteroseptal, anterior, lateral, posterior, inferior and inferoseptal walls ring the cavity in order, with one or two papillary muscles jutting inward. The right ventricle crescent sits beside it. This is the monitoring plane of anaesthesia practice because wall motion of every territory shows at once during surgery.

steps.en: What you see: Advanced into the stomach with the tip flexed upward, the probe looks back at the heart from below so the left ventricle appears as a round doughnut in cross section. The anteroseptal, anterior, lateral, posterior, inferior and inferoseptal walls ring the cavity in order, with one or two papillary muscles jutting inward. The right ventricle crescent sits beside it. This is the monitoring plane of anaesthesia practice because wall motion of every territory shows at once during surgery.

Landmarks to confirm: Left ventricle cavity in cross section, anteroseptal and inferoseptal walls, anterior, lateral, posterior and inferior walls, papillary muscles, right ventricle crescent, mid interventricular septum.

Common mistakes and correction: Too apical a cut with a small cavity that fakes hypertrophy: withdraw until the papillary muscles show clearly. Too basal a cut that includes the mitral apparatus: advance slightly past the valve. Off centre cut that makes one wall look thin and ischaemic: centre the cavity so all walls share the sector equally.

Normal values with units: Probe depth about 40 cm from the incisors in the stomach. Multiplane angle 0 degrees. In health every wall thickens toward the centre in systole and no territory lags behind. Left ventricular ejection fraction 52 percent or above in men and 54 percent or above in women marks the lower reference limit.

Pitfalls: Stomach gas can wipe out the inferior wall, so reposition and retry before calling wall motion abnormal. Excessive tip flexion presses the stomach wall and degrades the image, so use the least flexion that holds the plane. In patients with known varices, strictures or recent gastric surgery, seek senior advice before advancing the probe.

todo.en: How to get it step by step: Under anaesthesia with the airway secured per local protocol, advance the probe gently to about 40 cm from the incisors into the stomach. Flex the tip forward and withdraw slightly until the mid papillary cross section appears. Keep the multiplane at 0 degrees and centre the cavity so the walls share equal thickness around the ring. If the mitral valve appears, the cut sits too basal, so advance a little. If the cavity shrinks toward a point, the cut sits too apical, so withdraw a little.

q.en: How is the transgastric mid short axis obtained?

o.en: Mid oesophagus at 30 cm with 0 degrees
Stomach at about 40 cm with forward flexion at 0 degrees
Upper oesophagus at 20 cm with 90 degrees

why.en: The probe advances to about 40 cm in the stomach with forward flexion at 0 degrees.

q.en: The mitral valve appears in the cross section. What does this mean?

o.en: Mitral valve in view means the cut sits too basal

why.en: Valve tissue in the ring means the cut sits too basal and the probe should advance slightly.

q.en: The cavity looks tiny with thick walls. What is the first correction?

o.en: Withdraw until the papillary muscles show clearly

why.en: A tiny cavity means too apical a cut, so withdraw until the mid papillary plane opens.
